`utls.Config` and `tls.Config` are same structs, aside for a type.

> create a utls.Config from an existing tls.Config

If you believe that it is generally useful , I wouldn't object to a PR that generates `tls.Config` from `utls.Config` by doing a deep copy. However, that code doesn't really have to be in the uTLS: user has access to all the fields of both `Config`s.

It's not as easy as it seems at first, because
* The version of crypto/tls may not match the version of utls, so their `Config` structs may not have the same fields.
* Not only the types of `tls.Config` and `utls.Config` are incompatible, but also some of their fields. For example, if you try to assign `utlsConfig.Certificates = tlsConfig.Certificates`, you get an error because each is defined in terms of its own `Certificate` type:
  ```
  cannot use tlsConfig.Certificates (type []"crypto/tls".Certificate) as type []"github.com/refraction-networking/utls".Certificate in assignment
  ```
For me, a perfect 1:1 clone isn't necessary. I can just try not to use the fields that have problems. I worked out a demo using a [reflection trick](https://groups.google.com/d/msg/Golang-Nuts/SDiGYNVE8iY/89hRKTF4BAAJ) that copies public fields that have a compatible type.

<details>
<summary>Click to expand program</summary>

```
package main

import (
	"crypto/tls"
	"fmt"
	"net"
	"net/http"
	"os"
	"reflect"
	"strings"

	utls "github.com/refraction-networking/utls"
	"golang.org/x/net/http2"
)

// For each field in dst, copy the corresponding named fields from src that are
// setting and have the same type. The idea of copying structs via reflection
// comes from a post by Nick Craig-Wood:
// https://groups.google.com/d/msg/Golang-Nuts/SDiGYNVE8iY/89hRKTF4BAAJ
func copyPublicFields(dst, src interface{}) {
	dstValue := reflect.ValueOf(dst).Elem()
	dstType := dstValue.Type()
	srcValue := reflect.ValueOf(src).Elem()
	srcType := srcValue.Type()
	for i := 0; i < dstValue.NumField(); i++ {
		dstField := dstValue.Field(i)
		name := dstType.Field(i).Name

		if !dstField.CanSet() {
			fmt.Printf("%2v cannot set %v\n", i, name)
			continue
		}

		dstTypeField := dstType.Field(i)
		srcTypeField, ok := srcType.FieldByName(name)
		if !ok {
			fmt.Printf("%2v src missing field %q\n", i, name)
			continue
		}

		if dstTypeField.Type != srcTypeField.Type {
			fmt.Printf("%2v different types for field %q\n", i, name)
			continue
		}

		value := srcValue.FieldByName(name)
		fmt.Printf("%2v Set %v = %v\n", i, name, value)
		dstField.Set(value)
	}
}

func utlsConfigFromTLSConfig(tlsConfig *tls.Config) *utls.Config {
	utlsConfig := new(utls.Config)
	copyPublicFields(utlsConfig, tlsConfig)
	return utlsConfig
}

func dialTLS(network, addr string, tlsConfig *tls.Config) (net.Conn, error) {
	fmt.Printf("DialTLS %v %v %v\n", network, addr, tlsConfig)

	colonPos := strings.LastIndex(addr, ":")
	if colonPos == -1 {
		colonPos = len(addr)
	}
	tlsConfig.ServerName = addr[:colonPos]

	conn, err := net.Dial(network, addr)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	// Convert the *tls.Config to a *utls.Config for UClient.
	utlsConfig := utlsConfigFromTLSConfig(tlsConfig)
	uconn := utls.UClient(conn, utlsConfig, utls.HelloFirefox_Auto)
	err = uconn.Handshake()
	return uconn, err
}

func main() {
	// Use http2.Transport.DialTLS as an example of where the stdlib may
	// give us a *tls.Config that we have to convert into a *utls.Config.
	rt := http2.Transport{
		DialTLS: dialTLS,
	}
	req, err := http.NewRequest("GET", "https://golang.org/robots.txt", nil)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "error: %v\n", err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	resp, err := rt.RoundTrip(req)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "error: %v\n", err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	fmt.Printf("%v\n", resp.Status)
}
```

https://gitlab.com/yawning/obfs4/commit/4d453dab2120082b00bf6e63ab4aaeeda6b8d8a3
It uses an I idea I didn't think of. Instead of setting `DialTLS` on an `http.Transport` and using it directly, it uses a wrapper `http.RoundTripper`. On the first dial, the wrapper initiates the `UClient` connection, then inspects `conn.ConnectionState().NegotiatedProtocol`. Depending on the negotiated protocol, it creates internally either an `http.Transport` or `http2.Transport`. Future dials are passed through to the internal transport directly.

Note that my implementation makes certain assumptions that may not be valid for a more general wrapper (omits some locking, destination host is assumed to be static), but there's comments where I do such things, and altering the behavior should be trivial.

Looking at [the example](https://github.com/refraction-networking/utls/pull/20/files#diff-1f008566bc39eeadf765a2d47f5836e4), it looks like the API is:
- Make a TCP connection.
- Call `UClient` with `HelloRandomized`/`HelloRandomizedALPN`/`HelloRandomizedNoALPN` and save the result.
- The call to `UClient` implicitly generates a randomized `ClientHelloID`.
- You can then make a second connection with the same fingerprint as the first, by calling `UClient` with the `ClientHelloID` generated by the first connection, in place of `HelloRandomized`/`HelloRandomizedALPN`/`HelloRandomizedNoALPN`.

It's surprising to me that you need to make a connection in order to generate a randomized fingerprint as a side effect. I think most real code is unlike the example in that there isn't a clear idea of which call to `UClient` is "first": instead, it will be called in a loop, or after a timeout. So in practice every call will have to have a check (actually much like [the check](https://github.com/refraction-networking/utls/pull/20/files#diff-17a6357df708d056c23f2eb7f0c63069R481) in `generateRandomizedSpec`) "Is this the first call? If so, use `HelloRandomized`. Otherwise, use the previous `ClientHelloID`." I was expecting something more like a factory function that I can call and it will produce a randomized `ClientHelloID` without making a connection, something like `generateRandomizedSpec` but as a public function. With the API as it is, I would be tempted to make a dummy localhost connection and throw it away, just for the sake of getting a randomized fingerprint that doesn't require case-checking later on.

What do you think about allowing the caller to supply their own `io.Reader` or `math/rand.Source` for random bits, instead of hardcoding `crypto/rand` and `math/rand`? Alright, I implemented SHA256 HKDF-based RNG for the randomized fingerprints in 79a37cfb6e8de35ea0df006ee8ec45b673db6319  
Everyone is welcome to provide an opinion, but I am especially interested to know if @rod-hynes considers this RNG strong enough to start using stock utls

Now the 63 bits of the seed are used (as opposed to previously used rand.NewSource() function, which takes int64 and then rounds it down to int32 throwing away precious entropy). I am not really concerned about entropy of 63 bit seed, tbh. For one, censor couldn't store so many fingerprints: even if every fp took only one byte (it takes way more than that, and if some of those fingerprints are the same, you'd have to store info about which ones are the same, which is still more than 1 byte), it'd take
```Golang
(2^63) bytes = 9223372.04 terabytes
```

As Yawning pointed out, there are some deficiencies in this implementation including using modulus for `Intn`. Decent explanation here: https://stackoverflow.com/a/6852396.

You could fix this, but I strongly echo the recommendation to implement your CSPRNG as a `rand.Source64` (https://golang.org/pkg/math/rand/#Source64) and then create a `rand.Rand` using that source to get correct implementations of all the helpers.

The issue with the max number of bytes that may be read from HKDF concerns me. We use a chacha20 stream cipher.

As for forking, we're undecided. If you use `rand.Source64` internally, then we could make a very simple change in a fork in order to keep using our CSPRNG.  This has one benefit for us, in that existing Psiphon client that have persisted a seed for a working random TLS fingerprint may continue to generate the same fingerprint after we upgrade `utls` (for some cases, and depending on whether the order of calls to `rand.Rand` remain the same as before). If we go this route we could contribute a code change that enables this customization.

I'm not clear on the seed size argument.

> since if your image space [...] exceeds 2^64 by a large amount, it's trivial for a censor to tell if something is one of the 2^64 uTLS-generated "randomized" fingerprints vs not

What's the trivial attack? I assume it's not storing all fingerprints, as you pointed out?

In any case, we have a 256-bit seed at present and so downgrading that vs. minor fork customization is another consideration.

For the record, there remains a number of other small, unrelated customizations we probably need and will maintain a fork for. Ultimately I'd like to see everything upstream and use stock `utls`.

The "trivial" attack for a censor to tell if something is one of the 2^64 fingerprints is not to store all the fingerprints, but to use a bloom filter to test if a given fingerprint is in the larger set. The censor could also maintain subsets of the 2^64 fingerprints and match probabilisticly.  Still an impractically large size for naive implementations, but I'll note that no sane cryptographic system uses 64-bits of security. If there's an easy way we could generate more than 2^64, we should. Otherwise, it's likely easier to block in other ways (e.g. keep state per client and observe multiple non-standard fingerprints).

https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5746
```
   This document defines a new TLS extension, "renegotiation_info" (with
   extension type 0xff01), which contains a cryptographic binding to the
   enclosing TLS connection (if any) for which the renegotiation is
   being performed.  The "extension data" field of this extension
   contains a "RenegotiationInfo" structure:

      struct {
          opaque renegotiated_connection<0..255>;
      } RenegotiationInfo;

   The contents of this extension are specified as follows.

   o  If this is the initial handshake for a connection, then the
      "renegotiated_connection" field is of zero length in both the
      ClientHello and the ServerHello.  Thus, the entire encoding of the
      extension is ff 01 00 01 00.  The first two octets represent the
      extension type, the third and fourth octets the length of the
      extension itself, and the final octet the zero length byte for the
      "renegotiated_connection" field.

   o  For ClientHellos that are renegotiating, this field contains the
      "client_verify_data" specified in Section 3.1.

   o  For ServerHellos that are renegotiating, this field contains the
      concatenation of client_verify_data and server_verify_data.  For
      current versions of TLS, this will be a 24-byte value (for SSLv3,
      it will be a 72-byte value).
```

Major browsers usually just specify a single 0x00 byte as a body of this renegotiation extension, so the entire extension ends up being `ff 01 00 01 00` where `ff 01` is extension type, `00 01` is length of extension body, and `00` is the body. `00` is actually also a length of the inner body, so the real body payload starts at offset 5.
That's where the `[]byte{0}` body case comes from: we want the right default. I am not sure under which circumstances browsers actually send the verify data.

If user specified the body explicitly, they presumably know what they're doing, so I tried to copy the body they specified into the extension. It seems like I didn't do this case correctly. The right thing to export would be `client_verify_data` and `server_verify_data`. When they're unset, it marshals to `ff 01 00 01 00`, otherwise it also concats the client verify data, sets the lengths to appropriate values, and verify the server verify data.
But the problem is that then we have to actually verify and implement the logic. You are welcome to implement this logic, if it is important in your circumvention operations. Otherwise, perhaps, RenegotiationExtension should not have any exported values in order to avoid the user a false impression that uTLS will verify what client is supposed to verify: that server's ServerHello will echo the RenegotiationExtension and the appropriate body in it. > As it creates two goroutine for reading and writing messages, there is no guarantee that Write() being called before Read(). I was just bitten by this problem as well, in the same situation: a pair of read/write goroutines started immediately after calling `UClient`. Calling `Handshake` before the first `Read` or `Write` is an effective workaround, but the silent failure to apply the chosen fingerprint is unexpected. I agree with @HirbodBehnam that it would be more natural if the connection works the same whether `Read` or `Write` is called first. Particularly as users of utls will be accustomed to the way [`Conn.Handshake`](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/tls#Conn.Handshake) works in crypto/tls; I read the documentation of `Conn.Handshake` and assumed utls would work the same way: > Most uses of this package need not call Handshake explicitly: the first Read or Write will call it automatically. Here is a running example of the network communication pattern I was using. I do not think it is anything too unusual. You can run, for example, `go run demo.go -- example.com:443` and then type `GET / HTTP/1.0\n\n` to get an HTTP response from the server—but the ClientHello will have the wrong TLS fingerprint. This is using go1.15.9 and utls v1.0.0.

	"flag"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"net"
	"os"
	"sync"

	"github.com/refraction-networking/utls"
)

func utlsDial(network, addr string, config *tls.Config) (*tls.UConn, error) {
	conn, err := net.Dial(network, addr)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	uconn := tls.UClient(conn, config, tls.HelloChrome_83)
	// err = uconn.Handshake()
	// if err != nil {
	// 	uconn.Close()
	// 	return nil, err
	// }
	return uconn, nil
}

func demo(addr string) error {
	serverName, _, err := net.SplitHostPort(addr)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	tlsConfig := tls.Config{ServerName: serverName}
	uconn, err := utlsDial("tcp", addr, &tlsConfig)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer uconn.Close()

	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	wg.Add(2)
	go func() {
		defer wg.Done()
		_, err := io.Copy(os.Stdout, uconn)
		if err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "stdout←uconn: %v\n", err)
		}
	}()
	go func() {
		defer wg.Done()
		_, err := io.Copy(uconn, os.Stdin)
		if err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "uconn←stdin: %v\n", err)
		}
	}()
	wg.Wait()

	return nil
}

func main() {
	flag.Parse()
	if flag.NArg() != 1 {
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%s: need a target host:port\n", os.Args[0])
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	err := demo(flag.Arg(0))
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}

After looking into this issue I found several problems. 

For uTLS, when we generate and send key shares in a ClientHello message, they are saved to a `*KeySharesParameters` to be retrieved later, while the first non-GREASE key share is copied and saved directly in the handshake states.

https://github.com/refraction-networking/utls/blob/fc79497d3f1c0f25f1ceb6672c3772b79b99c30f/u_parrots.go#L2433-L2477

However in `(*UConn).clientHandshake`, the `*KeySharesParameters` was mistakenly overridden by a `NewKeySharesParameters()`. 

https://github.com/refraction-networking/utls/blob/fc79497d3f1c0f25f1ceb6672c3772b79b99c30f/u_conn.go#L566-L571

It caused us to lose all but the first key share (saved elsewhere).

For the target host `pbs.twimg.com` however, they have at least 2 sets of configurations, TLS12-only and TLS13-compatible. 

For the TLS12-only ones, the connection WILL not fail as the server selects `x25519`, the first advertised Key Share. The other group, TLS13-compatible servers will instead select `secp256r1`, the second, which is lost as mentioned. 

This problem happens ONLY if we advertise more than one key share at the same time (Firefox's default behavior). Advertising **the support of** more than one key share (through `supported_groups` extension) does not cause any issue.

- If `RealPSKResumption` is set to true: parsing from raw bytes will discard the ticket and binders from the raw bytes, but use the available ones from `ClientSessionCache` instead.

The `SessionController` was designed to manage all session-related operations. Initially, it had ownership over extensions. 

But this posed a challenge. The ClientHelloSpec might have a different set of PSK/Session extensions. For clarity, the original design had the `SessionController` take charge of the extensions, overwriting those from the spec. This leads to the design that `newSessionController` produces a non-nil session and a psk extension. A downside of this approach was that it altered the signature of a public method, and we didn't have a clear vision for v2.0 yet.

To circumvent this, I pivoted to a strategy where the Spec owns the extensions, ensuring the method signature remains unchanged. However, users should be able to override psk/session extensions before invoking `ApplyPreset`. These overriding extensions should exclusively reside in the `SessionController`. In such cases, the `SessionController` have ownership over the extensions.

This necessitated the creation of the `syncSessionExts` method to discern which extension takes precedence. The guiding principle is straightforward:

1. If both the user and the spec offer an extension, prioritize the user's.
2. If the spec lacks an extension and the user attempts to provide one, it's deemed an error.
3. In the absence of a user-provided extension, revert to the spec's version, if available.

Yet, during this overhaul, I overlooked the `newSessionController` method. As illustrated in the comments, deep in my mind I believe that the extension would default to nil unless overridden by the user:

While this  #348 appears to fix the issue by handling the `compress_certificate` extension, the underlying problem is a difference in how we handle handshake transcripts compared to the standard `crypto/tls` library.

The standard library writes raw message bytes directly to the transcript hash. In contrast, `uTLS` often relies on `unmarshal` and `marshal` to reconstruct the message bytes. The `unmarshal` function ignores extensions it doesn't recognize, leading to an incorrect transcript.
